name: TigerBeetle
summary: A replicated database with one fixed schema, double-entry accounts and transfers, built in Zig to record money movements at high rates with strict serializability.
intro: TigerBeetle doesn’t store arbitrary tables. It has two kinds of record: accounts, grouped into ledgers such as a currency, and transfers, each of which debits one account and credits another on the same ledger by an amount. Accounts keep running totals of posted and pending debits and credits, from which the application computes balances, and can be told never to let debits exceed credits. Both records are immutable once created, fixed at 128 bytes, and carry a `code` for the reason and three indexed `user_data` fields for the application’s own IDs. Transfers can be linked so a group succeeds or fails together, as in a currency exchange, and two-phase transfers reserve an amount as pending first, then post all or part of it, void it, or let it time out.

It is built for the write-heavy, contended side of transaction processing, where a few accounts, such as a bank’s settlement account, take part in most transfers and row locks in a general-purpose database queue up. Requests always arrive in batches of up to 8,190 events, which a single leader applies one after another on one core, with no locks; the cost of replication is paid once per batch. Memory is allocated once at startup, I/O goes through Linux `io_uring`, and data lives in a forest of LSM trees. The vendor’s guidance is to keep a general-purpose database such as PostgreSQL for the slower-changing data, and put the money movements in TigerBeetle.

A cluster replicates with Viewstamped Replication and can be spread across three clouds, two replicas in each, so it survives losing a whole provider. Every piece of data is checksummed and hash-chained, so a replica detects a corrupted sector and repairs it from the others. The code is tested by the VOPR, a deterministic simulator that runs the real cluster under network, disk and process faults. A Jepsen analysis in 2025 found it met its strict serializability claim from 0.16.26 onward, after fixes to several crashes and two safety bugs.
strengths: Debits and credits are the database’s own primitives, so balances can’t drift and every change is an immutable transfer
High throughput on hot accounts: batches of up to 8,190 transfers applied without row locks
Strict serializability with automatic failover, checked by Jepsen and by continuous simulation testing
Built to survive disk corruption and the loss of a whole cloud provider
limits: Only accounts and transfers: everything else, such as customer details, needs a second database
Records are immutable, so corrections are new transfers, and changing a ledger’s scale means creating a new ledger
Throughput comes from one leader on one core; more replicas add safety, not speed
Requests are retried forever by default, which Jepsen flagged as making errors hard to tell apart from slowness

goodFor.why: Linked transfers succeed or fail together, and the cluster is strictly serializable, as Jepsen confirmed from 0.16.26 onward.
Transfers arrive in batches of up to 8,190, applied on one core without row locks, so hot accounts don’t queue on locks.

specs.data-model: Fixed schema: accounts and transfers, 128 bytes each, immutable
specs.transactions: Batches of up to 8,190 events; linked events succeed or fail together
specs.scaling: One leader on one core; more replicas add safety, not speed
specs.multi-region: Can span three clouds with two replicas in each
specs.storage-engine: A forest of LSM trees, checksummed and hash-chained

story: In 2020 Joran Dirk Greef, consulting for Coil, studied the safety and performance of Mojaloop, an open-source payments switch, with Adrian Hope-Bailie and Donovan Changfoot. They found many ad hoc ledgers built on general-purpose databases that topped out around 2,000 transactions a second. TigerBeetle began in July 2020 as a drop-in open-source database to power such a switch; Coil released it under Apache 2.0, and the first prototype reached about 200,000 transactions a second.

The team wrote it in Zig, then a young language, for control over memory allocation and tight latency bounds, and built it around Viewstamped Replication and deterministic simulation testing from the start. Coil spun TigerBeetle out as a company, which raised a $6.4 million seed round led by Amplify Partners in January 2023.

Jepsen tested versions 0.16.11 to 0.16.30 in 2025 and found it met its strict serializability claim once its bugs were fixed. In March 2026 the team reported processing a trillion transactions in a test cluster that kept its lower LSM levels in object storage.

choices.why: Double-entry bookkeeping is centuries old and fits every money movement. Making it the only data model lets the database enforce balance rules and pack each transfer into 128 bytes.

choices.choice: Batches on one core instead of row locks
choices.why: Payment workloads hammer a few hot accounts, where locking serialises everything anyway. Applying large batches in order on one thread removes lock contention and pays for replication once per batch.
Greef argues VSR, published before Paxos and revised before Raft, elects the next primary in a fixed round-robin order and copes better than Raft when the most up-to-date replica has a faulty disk.

Allocating all memory at startup rules out out-of-memory errors and fragmentation, and a deterministic codebase can be replayed exactly in the VOPR simulator, which injects faults at many times real speed.
